note: Per-paper few-shot paragraphs (~150-250 words each) compiled by subagent from top-10K excerpts. Each paragraph includes (a) what the paper studies, (b) the LHS DV(s), (c) the estimator, (d) any RHS log confounders, (e) data structure (panel/cross-section/RCT/etc.), (f) treatment design, (g) strict-heterogeneity assessment, (h) confounders a careful reader could be misled by. Paired with the audited ground-truth verdicts in data/llm_verdicts_groundtruth/ for few-shot encoding.

papers.role: Clean log-DV — spatial RDD, China environmental regulation
papers.paragraph: This QJE paper estimates the productivity cost of China's water-quality regulation using a spatial regression discontinuity around water-quality monitoring stations, where upstream firms face tighter enforcement than nearby downstream firms. The treatment is a policy intervention that imposes significant abatement costs on regulated firms — they install scrubbers, reduce production, or switch inputs to comply, so the intervention is costly per firm treated. The main dependent variables are log(TFP) (estimated via Olley–Pakes), log(COD emissions), log(COD emission intensity), log(water input), and log(wastewater); coefficients are explicitly back-transformed as percentage effects via 'e^β − 1' (e.g., 'a TFP loss in the range of 29% (e^−0.34 − 1) to 32% (e^−0.38 − 1)'), confirming log-DV. The estimator is local-linear nonparametric RD with MSE-optimal bandwidth (Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik), clustered SEs at the station level, with industry and station fixed effects absorbed via the Lee–Lemieux two-step. The data combine firm-level Annual Survey of Industrial Firms records with the ESR emission registry and remote pollution-sensor readings from the water monitoring stations themselves (georeferenced environmental monitors), collapsed to a cross-section for the baseline RD but also exploited as a panel for a difference-in-discontinuities specification with firm FE. The treatment is a binary upstream-vs-downstream indicator at the cutoff; an IV using hydrological-station location is added for robustness. The split between polluting and non-polluting industries functions as a placebo/source-of-variation check, NOT as subject-level heterogeneous treatment effects, so heterogeneous_effects is no despite the appearance of 'heterogeneous treatment effect' wording.

This Econometrica paper is purely theoretical: it studies a continuous-time financial economy with asymmetric information in which an informed agent receives a private signal about the terminal payoff Ψ(X_T) of a diffusion, while an uninformed agent has general von Neumann–Morgenstern preferences (extending the standard CARA-Gaussian framework). The contribution is to prove existence of a partial communication equilibrium (PCE), show that in the single-asset case this PCE is a dynamic noisy rational expectations equilibrium, and derive a quasi-explicit (Lambert-function) solution for CRRA uninformed agents in the small- and large-risk-aversion limits. There are no data, no regressions, no empirical samples — only stochastic-analysis proofs, fixed-point arguments for the stochastic discount factor, and measurability arguments for parameter-driven stochastic integrals. Despite heavy mathematical machinery and discussions of equilibrium 'prices,' 'volatility,' and 'endowment effects,' nothing is estimated from observations. Consequently, is_empirical is no, log_dv_likely is no, transformation is none, and every estimator/design field (instrumental, panel, RDD, experimental, heterogeneous effects, dummy outcomes, etc.) is no. A careless reader could be misled by the asset-pricing vocabulary and the references to 'equilibrium price' and 'market price of risk,' but these are theoretical objects, not regression outputs.

This JPE paper studies whether rising low-skill labor costs induce automation innovation, using a firm-level panel of patent counts from EPO/PATSTAT classified as 'automation' via a dictionary method on machinery C/IPC codes. The main DV is the count of automation patents at the firm-year level, PAT_{Aut,i,t}, estimated by Poisson PML — explicitly: 'Since our dependent variable is a count of patents, we use a Poisson specification … we use the ppmlhdfe command from Correia, Guimarães, and Zylkin (2020), which allows us to run Poisson regression models with high-dimensional fixed effects.' Crucially, the right-hand side carries log(low-skill wages), log(high-skill wages), log(K_Aut), log(K_other), and log(spillovers) — these are RHS controls, not the DV; coefficients are read as elasticities because Poisson has a log link. Data are a firm × year panel 1997–2011 with firm, industry×year, and country×year fixed effects, SEs clustered at firm. Identification uses a shift-share / Bartik-style instrument on foreign wages (Borusyak–Hull–Jaravel) for the endogenous domestic wage shock — so the design is IV. Treatment is continuous (wage shocks), with auxiliary event-study on the Hartz reforms and a triple-difference comparing automation vs non-automation machinery patents. The auto-vs-non-auto split is a placebo across outcome types, and the minimum-wage / Hartz analyses are alternative shock sources — neither constitutes subject-subgroup heterogeneity, so heterogeneous_effects is no.

This QJE paper by Chetty, Friedman, Saez, Turner, and Yagan studies income segregation and intergenerational mobility across U.S. colleges using linked IRS, Department of Education, College Board, and ACT administrative records for the 1980–82 birth cohorts. Even though the paper discusses dollar incomes throughout — Ivy-Plus parents above $532,000, bottom-quintile families below $25,000 — every regression estimated has a percentile rank on the left-hand side, not a log. The main specification is an OLS rank-rank regression of the child's individual earnings percentile rank on the parent's household income percentile rank, with college fixed effects (and college × SAT/ACT bin FE in extensions): 'We assign children income percentiles by ranking them based on their individual earnings relative to other children in the same birth cohort.' Descriptive tabulations of working and marriage rates appear in the paper but are not used as regression outcomes; the only secondary specifications swap the LHS for household-income percentile rank, also not binary. There is no log transformation, no IV, no RDD, no experiment, no panel (a single cohort cross-section), and no costly intervention. Tables stratifying mobility statistics by college tier and parent-income quintile are descriptive stratification, not treatment-by-subgroup heterogeneity, so heterogeneous_effects is no. The classifier should NOT be fooled into setting log_dv_likely=yes by the pervasive dollar language; the DV is rank, hence transformation=none.

papers.role: Belgium tax compliance — binary DV with RCT + RDD + causal forests
papers.paragraph: This JPE paper runs four large natural field experiments with Belgium's tax administration testing simplification, deterrence, and tax-morale messages in letters sent to the universe of relevant taxpayers (TP, TPR, TF, TFR experiments, totaling several million observations). Main DVs are binary compliance outcomes — probability of timely payment, probability of filing within a deadline — estimated by linear probability models: 'Y_i = α + β_S S_i + Σ_j β_j T_j_i + γ X_i + ε_i,' with the dummy outcomes paid/filed within X days. In the Tax Filing (TF) experiment a secondary DV is reported taxable income in levels (also not logged). No log transformation appears on any LHS, so log_dv_likely is speculative at best and transformation=none. The design is a multi-arm RCT (simplified letter, simplified+deterrence, simplified+tax-morale, with several sub-variants) — so multiarm_treatment=yes and dummy_treatment=yes. A regression discontinuity at an enforcement-intensity tax-liability cutoff is layered on top of the experimental variation to benchmark simplification against enforcement, hence regression_discontinuity=yes. Heterogeneous_effects is yes here because the paper does a dedicated subject-subgroup analysis using causal forests (Wager–Athey) interacting treatment with taxpayer characteristics (age, children, liability, solvency) — this is genuine HTE on subject covariates, distinct from the multi-arm letter splits. The repeated TPR rounds across FY2014/FY2015 give a repeated cross-section flavor at the experiment level; a few robustness specifications exploit within-taxpayer variation across rounds with taxpayer fixed effects, supporting at least a speculative panel reading. Alongside the administrative tax records, the paper also draws on a separate tax-morale survey of taxpayers to measure compliance attitudes.

papers.role: Rohingya refugee RCT — multi-arm linear, NOT heterogeneity
papers.paragraph: This AER paper presents a pre-registered three-arm field experiment with 745 Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh estimating the psychosocial value of employment. The arms are (1) pure control, (2) weekly cash of equivalent value, and (3) gainful employment (a surveying job ~3 days/week for 8 weeks) — a classic multi-arm RCT (multiarm_treatment=yes, dummy_treatment=yes, costly_intervention=yes given the real wages paid). The main DV is a standardized psychosocial-wellbeing index, estimated linearly (ITT comparisons across arms); there is no log transformation, so log_dv_likely=no and transformation=none. The setting is a single-period field experiment, not a panel in the standard entity×time econometric sense (though there are repeated weekly survey waves), so panel=speculative. The abstract notes 'effects concentrated among males,' which suggests gender heterogeneity, but the top-10K excerpt only states this in passing and does not lay out a dedicated treatment-by-subject-characteristic heterogeneity specification — hence heterogeneous_effects=speculative rather than yes. The classifier must NOT confuse the cash-vs-work arm comparison with heterogeneous effects: that comparison is a multi-arm treatment contrast (isolating the non-pecuniary channel), not a subject-covariate interaction. Specifications include the usual demographic controls (age, gender, marital status) and baseline psychosocial-index values, supporting at least a speculative 'lots_of_controls' reading. No IV, no RDD, no log DV.
